transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-11 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~78m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jon (Redwood SE), Aisha (Head of ML - Hyperion), Diego (Infra Lead), Priya (SRE)

Summary: Quick alignment on apples-to-apples benchmark protocol for Hyperion's routing/fulfillment LLMs, agreed to run replay-based benchmarks with three model sizes, and validate KV cache sizing and batching windows under production-like burst. Action items captured.

Topics: KV cache sizing, batching policy, quantization profiles, load replay methodology, VPC/on-prem constraints, acceptable quality degradation thresholds.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll keep this fairly technical — Jon and I want to walk through a reproducible protocol so your infra team can validate performance on-prem.
[00:14] Aisha: Thanks — we really need apples-to-apples numbers. Our concern is previous vendor numbers include very different prompt mixes.
[00:23] Jon: Totally. We'll start with the prompt set discussion then go into load generation and what "apples-to-apples" means for batching and KV cache. Quick check — you shared a 7-day trace, yes?
[00:33] Diego: Yep, sent it as link. It's a mix of short status queries (~40% of tokens), medium prompts for route planning (~45%), and long contextual prompts for manifests (~15%).
[00:46] Jon: Good, that's helpful. For KV cache discussion: first principle, cache hit rate is a function of sequence reuse and session stickiness. For Hyperion your route planning has high reuse, so we can tune for high KV hit rates.
[01:05] Priya: Interruption — when you say "high hit rate" what numbers should we expect? 80, 90?
[01:10] Jon: We're seeing 60-85% in similar fleets when user sessions persist across multiple calls. With prefix caching and sticky routing you'd aim for 70%+; worst-case cold-starts for new shipments, it'll dip to 20-30% until warmed.
[01:25] Diego: Okay that maps. Our session TTL is 12 hours, so warm is likely.
[01:30] Maya: On batching, important to standardize the batching window (e.g., 5-20ms) and max batch size. For low-latency route queries you probably want small window and smaller max batch to keep p95 latency low.
[01:46] Aisha: We need p95 < 200ms for route suggestions, but manifest generation can be 800-1k ms.
[01:52] Jon: So we'll specify per-workload SLOs in the protocol. For the benchmark we'll run three traffic classes: interactive (p95 target 200ms), transactional (p95 target 800ms), and background (throughput-focused).
[02:06] Maya: On quantization, Hyperion asked about 8-bit vs 4-bit tradeoffs — Jon, can you run through practical impacts?
[02:13] Jon: Sure. 8-bit (q8) typically yields ~1.6-2x speedup on GPU + small quality delta for most LLMs. 4-bit (q4) can be 2.5-3x but risks hallucination/regression on long-context prompts, especially manifests. So our protocol will include automatic quality checks — token-level perplexity and a small eval prompt set checking entity extraction and numeric fidelity.
[02:40] Diego: Are those evals open-source? We need to run inside our VPC.
[02:44] Jon: Yes — we'll provide the prompt set CSV and the eval harness you can run locally. It's the s3 link in the notes.
[02:52] Aisha: On load generation — we prefer replaying production traces if possible to match distribution. Synthetic loads were misleading in prior POCs.
[02:59] Jon: Agreed. Replay is best for hitting the right mix and tail behavior — but we need to normalize request pacing so the cluster sees the same rate profile. Protocol step-by-step: 1) sanitize trace (remove PII), 2) map request types to workload class, 3) replay with clock-aligned scaling factor to hit target QPS, 4) run warm-up period to prefill KV caches.
[03:20] Priya: How long should warm-up be?
[03:22] Jon: For your traffic I'd recommend 30-60 minutes of steady-state warm-up, until key hit-rate stabilizes, then run the benchmark for 1 hour min to capture diurnal burst patterns.
[03:37] Maya: Also important — quantization and kernel selection must be consistent across comparative runs. If comparing q8 on Redwood vs q8 on another vendor, ensure both runs use the same tokenizer, model weights, sequence length caps, and sampling parameters.
[03:54] Aisha: This is where apples-to-apples trips people up — same prompt + different sampling temp will change latency and token counts.
[04:02] Jon: Exactly. Our protocol will include a strict runbook file — model hash, tokenizer version, decode params, input truncation rules.
[04:10] Diego: For private deployment, network overhead matters. When we tested a hosted vendor before, the extra hop to the cloud added ~20ms median — we need to quantify that for our VPC option.
[04:20] Jon: We'll instrument both e2e and intra-node latencies. For on-prem we capture kernel queue times, PCIe transfer, and GPU compute. For hosted we capture network RTT + e2e. Protocol has a "latency decomposition" section.
[04:33] Maya: Let's pivot to measurement specifics — token-level timing, p50/p95/p99, and per-route breakdowns. We'll also track batching window distribution and per-batch size histogram.
[04:45] Aisha: Will you provide dashboards? Our SRE wants per-minute charts.
[04:49] Jon: Yes we'll share a Grafana dashboard template and the CSV exporter for offline analysis.
[04:56] Priya: Anything else about KV cache sizing? Memory footprint on GPU is a constraint for us.
[05:00] Jon: Right — KV cache size scales roughly with (context length * hidden_size * bytes_per_param) per session. We'll include a calculator in the protocol. For example, 8k context with 4k sessions => X GB of GPU memory. We'll simulate session concurrency in the replay to check OOM risk.
[05:20] Diego: Good, OOM is our biggest fear.
[05:22] Jon: We'll run an early safety pass at slow QPS to exercise cache growth, then the full load.
[05:29] Maya: Ok, let's walk through a sample execution plan live — Jon, can you outline the four phases we'll run during Redwood-assisted benchmark?
[05:36] Jon: Phase 0: Sanitize and categorise trace. Phase 1: Warm-up 45m with KV prefilling. Phase 2: Baseline run (no quantization change) 60m. Phase 3: Variant runs — q8 and q4, each 60m with the same replay seed and pacing. Collect all metrics and run quality checks.
[05:56] Aisha: And for apples-to-apples vs competitor, we need the competitor to run the exact same trace and steps. We can share the sanitized trace with them under NDA.
[06:05] Maya: We'll note that as an option.
[06:08] Priya: A few clarifying Qs on batching windows: Do you recommend dynamic batching (adaptive) or fixed window?
[06:15] Jon: Adaptive batching works well when you have variable QPS — our runtime uses small adaptive windows that expand under mild burst to improve throughput while honoring latency SLO with per-route knobs. For this protocol, we capture two modes: fixed conservative window (e.g., 5ms) and adaptive mode. We compare both.
[06:33] Diego: For throughput numbers, do you normalize by token or by request?
[06:36] Jon: Both. Tokens/sec and requests/sec matter. We'll report both and cost-per-token.
[06:41] Aisha: Regarding quality checks — what metrics exactly? Perplexity, entity extraction F1, and numeric closeness?
[06:47] Jon: Yes. We'll run model outputs through a small eval harness: 1) perplexity delta vs baseline, 2) extraction F1 on labelled prompts, 3) numeric rounding accuracy for manifests. If q4 degrades beyond thresholds (e.g., F1 drop >5% or numeric error >2%), we mark it as failure.
[07:05] Diego: Noted. How about hidden caveats — say different CUDA/cuDNN versions across on-prem testbeds?
[07:12] Jon: We'll standardize the driver/kernel matrix in the runbook — recommend minimal tested driver versions; we'll also include a hardware compatibility checklist.
[07:22] Priya: Anything on security / compliance for private runs?
[07:25] Maya: We'll provide SOC2 artifact pack and a private deployment checklist including KMS/HSM integration notes and audit logs. Diego, I think you'll want RBAC for route access?
[07:34] Diego: Yes. We need per-team isolation and auditability.
[07:37] Maya: Great — we'll include that in the docs we send.
[07:40] [07:40] Aisha: Slight tangent — can Redwood's runtime do automatic fallback to smaller model if under heavy load? That was in your docs.
[07:48] Jon: Yes. Smart routing can route by policy — latency-first routes go to smaller low-latency model, cost route to larger model. For benchmarks we'll keep routing static to avoid confounding.
[07:58] Diego: Back to replay — how do you handle randomness in sampling for decode?
[08:01] Jon: We'll fix seeds when sampling to ensure deterministic outputs; for temperature-based decoding we'll provide both deterministic (greedy) and stochastic seeds but lock them per-run. That way quality diffs are attributable to quant and not sampling variance.
[08:15] Maya: Let's capture required artifacts from Hyperion to start: 1) sanitized replay trace, 2) target SLOs per route class, 3) baseline model hash / tokenizer, 4) access to a staging GPU for assisted runs.
[08:30] Diego: We'll try to provide the trace by 2026-04-15 and can allocate a small staging 4-GPU box for initial runs.
[08:38] Aisha: We also want end-to-end cost modeling — token cost + infra amortization.
[08:44] Jon: We'll export token-level cost calc; for private, we provide a per-hour GPU amortized cost template.
[08:51] Priya: Any suggestions on orchestration for on-prem? Helm charts? Operator?
[08:55] Jon: For on-prem we support Helm-based install and a lightweight operator for GPU rounds; we'll deliver the chart for dry-run.
[09:02] Diego: Good.
[09:04] [09:04] Short silence / file shuffle
[09:15] Aisha: Can we run a small sanity test now — like a 5-minute smoke with q8 to see basic p50 numbers?
[09:20] Jon: We can but given this is a recorded meeting I'll note we agreed to a later hands-on session. Let's schedule the smoke for next week during the dry-run.
[09:28] Maya: Recap: Redwood to provide runbook, eval harness, dashboards, and pricing. Hyperion to provide trace, SLOs, and staging infra. Redwood SE to run initial replay and share histograms.
[09:41] Diego: Sounds good. Also include network baseline numbers for our VPC path.
[09:46] Maya: Will do.
[09:48] [End of call — wrap-up and informal chatter about lunch spots]

Notes about transcription quality: occasional garbling on model names (e.g., q8/q4 heard as "cue eight/for") and speaker overlap around 00:56-01:02. Some proper nouns may be slightly off.

Additional context: Hyperion is balancing very low-latency interactive routing with high-throughput batch manifests. The benchmark protocol aims to expose tradeoffs and produce a clear cost/latency/quality frontier.
